```{r}
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
files <- readLines("inputs.txt")
all <- rbindlist(lapply(files, fread), fill = TRUE)
all[, input := paste(norm, feat, sep = " / ")]
# facet labels: module ids without the parameter hash
all[, NORM := sub("\\..*$", "", norm)][, FEAT := sub("\\..*$", "", feat)]
all[, basis := fifelse(grepl("nmf", pca), "NMF", "PCA")]
# localisation rows are per arm, the reference included; accuracy rows exclude it
loc <- all[metric %in% c("ipr", "ipr_floor")]
ve <- all[metric == "var_explained"]
pa <- unique(all[metric == "pa_edge" & is_reference == TRUE, .(NORM, FEAT, input, edge = 100 * value)])
m <- all[is_reference == FALSE & !metric %in% c("ipr", "ipr_floor", "var_explained", "pa_edge")]
# log axes: exact agreement is 0, show it at the double-precision floor
floor_ <- 1e-16
m[, shown := pmax(value, floor_)]
# NMF is not a PCA basis (not orthogonal, not variance-ordered): per-PC and
# eigenvalue rows compare unrelated factors, so those plots leave it out
sci <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "e", digits = 1)
```

Every PCA arm is compared with `pc_exact` (scanpy, dense LAPACK SVD, float64)
computed on **the same** `normalized_selected` matrix: same dataset, NORM and
FEAT branch. Sines come from projection residuals, so values down to ~1e-15
are real. NMF factors are neither orthogonal nor ordered by variance: read only
their subspace rows.

`r m[, uniqueN(pca)]` PCA modules, `r m[, uniqueN(input)]` input matrices,
`r m[, uniqueN(dataset)]` dataset(s), from `r length(files)` metric table(s).

## Summary

```{r}
s <- m[, .(
  `max pc_sin, PC1-10` = max(value[metric == "pc_sin" & index <= 10]),
  `subspace_sin k=10` = value[metric == "subspace_sin" & index == 10][1],
  `subspace_sin k=50` = value[metric == "subspace_sin" & index == 50][1],
  `max eig_rel_err, PC1-10` = max(value[metric == "eig_rel_err" & index <= 10])
), by = .(dataset, basis, pca, pca_params, input)]
setorder(s, dataset, basis, pca, input)
num <- names(s)[sapply(s, is.numeric)]
s[, (num) := lapply(.SD, sci), .SDcols = num]  # kable(digits=) would round 1e-13 to 0
knitr::kable(s, align = "l")
```

## Variance explained

Share of the FEAT matrix's total variance (sum of every gene's variance, not
of the 50 kept PCs) carried by each PC of `pc_exact`, and its cumulative sum.
Dotted line: the elbow from `PCAtools::findElbowPoint()` on that curve; it
only sees the 50 kept PCs. Red dashed line: the parallel-analysis noise edge
(95th percentile of the top eigenvalue after shuffling every gene across cells,
20 times; Horn 1965, in the permutation form of Buja & Eyuboglu 1992, with
Glorfeld's 1995 95th percentile). PCs above it carry structure; the bulk below
it is per-gene noise, which is why 50 PCs leave half the total variance
unexplained. This is the *edge* form: every PC is compared with the top
shuffled eigenvalue. Horn's original compares PC i with the i-th shuffled
eigenvalue (as `PCAtools::parallelPCA` does) and keeps slightly more; for the
first component the two coincide with the Tracy-Widom test (Saccenti &
Timmerman 2017).

```{r}
if (nrow(ve) == 0) {
  cat("No `normalized_selected_h5` was gathered, so total variance is unknown.\n")
} else {
  ref <- ve[is_reference == TRUE, .(PC = index, pct = 100 * value, NORM, FEAT, input)]
  ref[, cum := cumsum(pct), by = input]
  elb <- ref[, .(elbow = PCAtools::findElbowPoint(pct)), by = .(NORM, FEAT, input)]
  above <- merge(ref, pa, by = c("NORM", "FEAT", "input"))[, .(`PCs above PA edge` = sum(pct > edge),
                                                               `PA edge %` = edge[1]), by = input]
  tab <- merge(elb, ref[, .(`% PC1` = pct[PC == 1], `cum % 10 PCs` = cum[PC == 10],
                            `cum % 50 PCs` = cum[PC == max(PC)]), by = input], by = "input")
  tab <- merge(tab, above, by = "input", all.x = TRUE)
  knitr::kable(tab[, !"input"], digits = 1)
}
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-width: 11
if (nrow(ve) > 0) {
  ggplot(ref, aes(PC)) +
    geom_col(aes(y = pct), fill = "grey55", width = 0.8) +
    geom_line(aes(y = cum / 5), colour = "steelblue") +
    geom_vline(data = elb, aes(xintercept = elbow), linetype = "dotted") +
    geom_hline(data = pa, aes(yintercept = edge), linetype = "dashed", colour = "firebrick") +
    scale_y_continuous("% of total variance (bars)",
                       sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . * 5, name = "cumulative % (line)")) +
    facet_grid(NORM ~ FEAT) +
    theme_bw()
}
```

## Per-PC loading error

sin(angle) between each PC's loading vector and the reference's. Rising error
at high PCs is expected where the eigengap closes (PCs below the noise edge).

```{r}
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-width: 11
ggplot(m[metric == "pc_sin" & basis == "PCA"], aes(index, shown, colour = pca, group = interaction(pca, pca_params))) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  facet_grid(NORM ~ FEAT) +
  labs(x = "PC", y = "sin(angle) to reference", colour = "PCA module") +
  theme_bw()
```

## Leading-subspace error

Largest principal-angle sine between the leading k loadings (solid) and cell
scores (dashed) of each arm and the reference.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-width: 11
sub <- m[metric %in% c("subspace_sin", "scores_sin")]
ggplot(sub, aes(index, shown, colour = pca, linetype = metric,
                group = interaction(pca, pca_params, metric))) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  facet_grid(NORM ~ FEAT) +
  labs(x = "k (leading PCs)", y = "max sin(principal angle)", colour = "PCA module") +
  theme_bw()
```

## Eigenvalue error

Relative error of each PC's score variance against the reference eigenvalue.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-width: 11
ggplot(m[metric == "eig_rel_err" & basis == "PCA"], aes(index, shown, colour = pca, group = interaction(pca, pca_params))) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  facet_grid(NORM ~ FEAT) +
  labs(x = "PC", y = "relative eigenvalue error", colour = "PCA module") +
  theme_bw()
```

## Loading localisation (IPR)

Effective number of genes per factor, 1/IPR with IPR = sum l^4 / (sum l^2)^2.
Gene g carries lambda_i * l_g^2 of eigenvalue i, so a low value means that
PC's variance sits on few genes. Dashed: a random unit vector (n_genes / 3).
Arms that match the reference overlap it; IPR is unstable where PCs are
near-degenerate, and in log-normalised data a very localised PC is often a
single-gene noise axis rather than a rare population, so read it within a
panel, not across NORM branches.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-width: 11
eff <- loc[metric == "ipr", .(PC = index, eff_genes = 1 / value, pca, pca_params, is_reference, NORM, FEAT)]
fl <- unique(loc[metric == "ipr_floor", .(NORM, FEAT, eff_floor = 1 / value)])
ggplot(eff, aes(PC, eff_genes, colour = pca, group = interaction(pca, pca_params))) +
  geom_line(aes(linewidth = is_reference)) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 1.2, `FALSE` = 0.4), guide = "none") +
  geom_hline(data = fl, aes(yintercept = eff_floor), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  facet_grid(NORM ~ FEAT) +
  labs(x = "factor", y = "effective genes (1/IPR)", colour = "module (thick = pc_exact)") +
  theme_bw()
```

## References

- Horn JL (1965). A rationale and test for the number of factors in factor analysis. *Psychometrika* 30:179–185. [doi:10.1007/BF02289447](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02289447)
- Buja A, Eyuboglu N (1992). Remarks on parallel analysis. *Multivariate Behavioral Research* 27(4):509–540. [doi:10.1207/s15327906mbr2704_2](https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327906mbr2704_2)
- Glorfeld LW (1995). An improvement on Horn's parallel analysis methodology for selecting the correct number of factors to retain. *Educational and Psychological Measurement* 55(3):377–393.
- Saccenti E, Timmerman ME (2017). Considering Horn's parallel analysis from a random matrix theory point of view. *Psychometrika* 82:186–209. [doi:10.1007/s11336-016-9515-z](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-016-9515-z)
- Single-cell use of parallel analysis: `PCAtools::parallelPCA` (Blighe & Lun, Bioconductor); Lun A, *Choosing the number of PCs for denoising*, CRUK Cambridge Institute technical report ([pdf](https://content.cruk.cam.ac.uk/jmlab/gitlab/miscellaneous/technical-reports/pc-selection.pdf)).
- Elbow: `PCAtools::findElbowPoint`. Elbow methods are the most common PC choice in single-cell work (Zhuang H et al. 2022, findPC, *Bioinformatics* 38(10):2949).
- IPR: Plerou V et al. (2002). Random matrix approach to cross correlations in financial data. *Phys Rev E* 65:066126. On scRNA-seq, sparsity alone can localise eigenvectors: Aparicio L et al. (2020). *Patterns* 1(3):100035.
